title: Fast fashion
excerpt: Most operators overlook how Fast fashion drives unit economics and competitive moats at scale. Understanding its real-world mechanics reveals why.
author: Ava Morales

body.text: Most operators overlook how Fast fashion drives unit economics and competitive moats at scale. Understanding its real-world mechanics reveals why disciplined organizations outperform during market shifts.

Fast fashion is a business model in textile manufacturing where companies quickly create and sell clothing and footwear at affordable prices by replicating the latest fashion trends and designs using cheap and fast mass production techniques.
Multinational retailers that employ the fast fashion strategy include Shein, Temu, H&M, ASOS, Peacocks, Fashion Nova, Forever 21, Uniqlo, Edikted, Zaraand C&A.
As of 2026, 36% of clothing purchases worldwide are of the fast fashion category. The total market size of fast fashion clothing sales is estimated at $178 billion in sales per year.

Fast fashion brands have faced legal and regulatory issues due to alleged exploitation of labour, use of dangerous goods in their products, greenwashing their environmental impacts, and violations of intellectual property laws.
Business model
Fast fashion brands aim to put popular styles on the market as quickly as possible at a lower price than their competitors via optimized supply chains and quick response manufacturing methods.

These retailers produce and sell products in small batches, maintain surplus manufacturing capacity to adjust production levels, use category management organization, and are able to make substantial and immediate adjustments to manufacturing based on sales.
Fast fashion companies generally invest heavily in marketing, particularly via social media, using influencers and internet celebrities to promote their brand.

The supply chains force factories into price competition for fear of losing business. This decreases financial risk from brands in fast fashion, while taking advantage of poorly regulated labor laws in manufacturing companies. The business model overall depends on vulnerable workers that endure wage suppression and an unsafe work environment.
These unethical standards are capitalized when businesses bargain for extremely cheap prices with large expectations.
History

Before the 19th century, fashion was a laborious, time-consuming process that required sourcing raw materials like wool, cotton, or leather, weaving the natural fibers into fabric, and then fashioning the fabric into functional garments. However, the Industrial Revolution changed the world of fashion by introducing new technology like the sewing machine and textile machines.

As a result, clothes became cheaper and easier to make and buy. Localized dressmaking businesses emerged, catering to members of the middle class, and employing workroom employees along with garment workers, who worked from home for meager wages.
These dress shops were early prototypes of the so-called 'sweatshops' that would become the foundation for twenty-first-century clothing production.

Fast fashion originated with utility clothing and tailors who sold mass-produced affordable suits for men. In the 1960s, companies including Inditex and Chelsea Girl attained commercial acumen, but the brand Biba endured as a fast fashion icon.

Before the popularization of the fast fashion model, the fashion industry traditionally operated on a four-season cycle, with designers working months in advance to anticipate customer preferences. However, this approach underwent a significant transformation in the 1960s and 1970s, as the younger generations began to create new trends.
During this period there was still a clear distinction between luxury goods and High Street fashion.

Fast fashion grew during the late 20th century as the clothing industry adopted cheaper manufacturing techniques including more efficient supply chains, new quick response manufacturing methods, increased usage of low-cost labor from Asia, and cheaper petroleum-based synthetic fibers.
Fast fashion particularly came to the fore during the vogue for "Boho-chic" in the mid-2000s.

In the 2010s and 2020s, fast fashion trends spread quicker via social media services such as Instagram, Pinterest, and TikTok. Through the creation of promotional opportunities, such as haul videos from influencers, fast fashion companies have been able to advertise and market their clothing towards Generation-Z.
As haul videos provide an emotional trigger that stimulates impulse buying, fast fashion brands and Shein in particular, are able to motivate their customers to engage in purchasing.

This impulse purchasing is defined as overconsumption, which has led to an increase in the amount of clothing produced and allowed for clothing to be easily disposed of after a few wears. The increase in speed of production and trend cycles has been defined as ultra-fast fashion..
Many of the companies with a high social media presence, such as Shein, Fashion Nova, and PrettyLittleThing, promote ultra-fast fashion.
Industrialization and long-term economic growth

Nobel Prize winner and economist Arthur Lewis believes an agriculture sector and manufacturing sector are essential in market development. He calls this a "Dual Sector Model" theory. It explains that emerging markets grow by shifting low-productivity agriculture labor into higher productive manufacturing labor.

Economists apply this framework to the fast fashion industry as the manufacturing can serve as a starting point for industrialization. Through this shift, moving unskilled workers out of rural areas raises wages which ultimately can boost countries from poverty.

Economists additionally note that investments from fast fashion companies in poor countries support broader economic growth and help fund infrastructure necessary to support long term national development. For instance, Industry leaders draw parallels to Chinas rapid industrialization in the late 20th century, where millions of workers moved from rural farming to more productive urban jobs.
Now China has the worlds second largest economy. Economists argue that apparel manufacturing can similarly act as a catalyst to lift countries out of poverty.
Additionally, due to the massive scale, the fast fashion sector provides employment to roughly 60-70 million workers. Higher employment rates leads to more income that circulates in the economy.
Consumer experience

Classism involves prejudice based on a person's perceived social or economic situation. Opinions are formed about how many clothes someone has, what style they are wearing, or the quality of one's clothing. Fast fashion helps reduce classism by providing all individuals access to affordable clothing that is on trend.
This means that lower income consumers can wear similar pieces to their peers, reducing class based discrimination, even if they own less clothes overall.
Environmental impact

The high-volume and rapid-turnover model of fast fashion encourages consumers to purchase more clothes and replace them more frequently. According to the United Nations Environment Programme, consumers are buying approximately 60% more clothing than in the past while keeping garments for about half as long.
The organization also reports that the equivalent of one truckload of discarded textiles is landfilled or incinerated every second.

The catalyst for this extreme production of material can be traced to the idea of overconsumption. With the excessive intake of goods that exceeds the true need, overconsumption leads to Americans discarding 68 pounds worth of textiles, cloth, and clothing per year.
This piles up in landfills, which is made up of about 66% of clothing waste, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. Additionally, textiles accounted for 4% of municipal waste.

Environmental pressures occur throughout the textile supply chain, from fibre production and dyeing to manufacturing, transportation, use and disposal. A scientific review published in 2020 estimated that the fashion industry produces more than 92 million tonnes of waste and consumes approximately 79 trillion liters of water annually.

The review identified water consumption, chemical pollution, carbon emissions and textile waste as major environmental impacts associated with the industry. Furthermore, the fashion industry is estimated to contribute approximately 2-8% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

A 2024 study comparing fast-fashion and traditional jeans consumption estimated that the carbon footprint per wear of fast-fashion jeans was 11 times higher than that of traditional fashion consumption.

A 2026 life cycle assessment of fast-fashion polyester and cotton T-shirts found that polyester garments generally had higher environmental impacts than cotton garments, particularly in terms of greenhouse gas emissions. 10 kg for cotton T-shirts under the conditions examined.
It also found that extending the lifespan of garments could reduce their carbon emissions by approximately 50%, highlighting the environmental effects of short clothing lifespans.

The extensive use of synthetic fibers creates an additional source of pollution. Fast fashion companies are searching for man-made and synthetic materials such as polyester, cotton, and fiber. During the production, each material requires a significant amount of pesticides, fungicides, and chemicals that release harmful acidic gasses into the environment.

Additionally during the manufacturing process, the textile industry uses more than 15,000 different chemicals while spinning, weaving, dyeing, and completing the clothes. Synthetic garments release microplastic fibres during their production, wearing, washing, and disposal. According to the IUCN, these microplastics account for 35% of the microplastics present in the ocean.
